implementation_notes: The collection performs the whole idiom in one call: List<T>.RemoveAll(match) 'removes all the elements that match the conditions defined by the specified predicate' in a single traversal, compacting the survivors down, shortening the list and returning the number removed - there is no separate algorithm-plus-erase pair to compose, which is why this is a native realization rather than a wrapper. Hash-based sets have the per-entry equivalent (HashSet<T>.RemoveWhere) where no compaction is involved, and arrays, which have no RemoveAll, are handled by compacting over a Span<T> and slicing it (arr.AsSpan(0, count)) or by a manual write-index loop. Reach for LINQ Where(...).ToList() only when a new list is acceptable: it copies every survivor, allocates, and changes the collection identity.
pitfalls: List<T>.RemoveAll returns the number of elements removed, not a bool: code that treats it as success/failure reads wrong when nothing matched, and code that ignores it loses the count.

Arrays and IReadOnlyList<T> have no RemoveAll, and RemoveAt inside a loop shifts the tail per element (O(n*k)) while a forward for-loop over the list skips elements after a removal - compact over a Span<T> and slice it instead.
The predicate is a delegate invoked once per element: lambda captures allocate, and mutating the list from inside the predicate throws InvalidOperationException because the version counter changed.
Where(...).ToList() looks equivalent but is copy-out: it allocates a second list, breaks aliases, and doubles peak memory in a hot path.
sources: learn.microsoft.com, List<T>.RemoveAll(Predicate<T>) - 'Removes all the elements that match the conditions defined by the specified predicate', returns the number removed, and traverses the list from the beginning passing each element to the predicate: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.list-1.removeall
